difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY because it tests one concept (the Bayesian-network factorisation of a complete assignment) and needs only four table look-ups and a single product, in about a minute.
stem:
Given the following Bayesian Network consisting of four Bernoulli random variables and the associated conditional probability tables:

![Figure: Bayesian network with four nodes. U has directed edges to V and to W; V and W each have a directed edge to Z.](/pyq/2024/fig/Q64-1.png)

|  | $P(\cdot)$ |
|---|---|
| $U = 0$ | 0.5 |
| $U = 1$ | 0.5 |

|  | $P(V = 0 \mid \cdot)$ | $P(V = 1 \mid \cdot)$ |
|---|---|---|
| $U = 0$ | 0.5 | 0.5 |
| $U = 1$ | 0.5 | 0.5 |

|  | $P(W = 0 \mid \cdot)$ | $P(W = 1 \mid \cdot)$ |
|---|---|---|
| $U = 0$ | 1 | 0 |
| $U = 1$ | 0 | 1 |

|  |  | $P(Z = 0 \mid \cdot)$ | $P(Z = 1 \mid \cdot)$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $V = 0$ | $W = 0$ | 0.5 | 0.5 |
| $V = 0$ | $W = 1$ | 1 | 0 |
| $V = 1$ | $W = 0$ | 1 | 0 |
| $V = 1$ | $W = 1$ | 0.5 | 0.5 |

The value of $P(U = 1, V = 1, W = 1, Z = 1) =$ ______ (rounded off to **three** decimal places).

solution.quick: A Bayesian network's joint distribution factorises as each node given its parents: $P(U, V, W, Z) = P(U)\,P(V \mid U)\,P(W \mid U)\,P(Z \mid V, W)$. Reading one entry from each table gives $0.5 \times 0.5 \times 1 \times 0.5 = 0.125$. Answer: **0.125**.

steps.title: Read the parents of each node
steps.body:
From the graph:

| Node | Parents | CPT used |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $U$ | none (root) | $P(U)$ |
| $V$ | $U$ | $P(V \mid U)$ |
| $W$ | $U$ | $P(W \mid U)$ |
| $Z$ | $V, W$ | $P(Z \mid V, W)$ |

steps.title: Factorise the joint distribution
steps.body:
The chain rule, in the order $U, V, W, Z$, holds for any distribution:

$$P(u, v, w, z) = P(u)\,P(v \mid u)\,P(w \mid u, v)\,P(z \mid u, v, w).$$

The network states that each node is conditionally independent of its non-descendants given its parents. So $W \perp V \mid U$, which gives $P(w \mid u, v) = P(w \mid u)$, and $Z \perp U \mid (V, W)$, which gives $P(z \mid u, v, w) = P(z \mid v, w)$. Hence

$$P(u, v, w, z) = P(u)\,P(v \mid u)\,P(w \mid u)\,P(z \mid v, w).$$

steps.title: Look up the four CPT entries for U = 1, V = 1, W = 1, Z = 1
Multiply
steps.body:
$$P(U = 1, V = 1, W = 1, Z = 1) = 0.5 \times 0.5 \times 1 \times 0.5 = 0.125.$$

This is already exact to three decimal places. As a sanity check on the tables, the product formula summed over all $2^4 = 16$ assignments equals $1$.

solution.teaching:
**What a Bayesian network encodes.** A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) whose nodes are random variables. Each node $X_i$ comes with a conditional probability table (CPT) giving $P(X_i \mid \text{Parents}(X_i))$: one row per combination of parent values, and each row sums to 1. The graph also asserts a set of *conditional independences*: every variable is conditionally independent of its non-descendants given its parents.

**From the chain rule to the factorisation.** For an ordering of the variables that respects the arrows, the chain rule gives

$$P(X_1, \dots, X_n) = \prod_{i} P(X_i \mid X_1, \dots, X_{i-1}).$$

Each $X_i$ is independent of its earlier non-parent variables given its parents, so every factor collapses to its CPT:

$$P(X_1, \dots, X_n) = \prod_{i} P(X_i \mid \text{Parents}(X_i)).$$

So the probability of one **complete** assignment of all the variables is a product of one entry from each CPT, and no summation is needed. Summation (marginalisation, for example by variable elimination) is only needed when some variables are left unassigned, as in $P(Z = 1)$.

**Why this is efficient.** Four binary variables have a full joint table with $2^4 - 1 = 15$ free parameters. This network needs only $1 + 2 + 2 + 4 = 9$, one free number per CPT row.

**Back to this question.** The graph $U \to V$, $U \to W$, $V \to Z$, $W \to Z$ gives $P(U, V, W, Z) = P(U)\,P(V \mid U)\,P(W \mid U)\,P(Z \mid V, W)$. The query fixes all four variables, so we pick the entries $0.5$, $0.5$, $1$ and $0.5$ and multiply to get $0.125$. Notice also that $W$ is a deterministic copy of $U$ (its CPT is the identity), and $V$ does not actually depend on $U$ (both rows of its CPT are equal).
solution.commonTrap: Forgetting the root prior $P(U = 1) = 0.5$ and multiplying only the three conditional entries, which gives $0.25$. Other slips are reading the $P(W = 0 \mid \cdot)$ column instead of $P(W = 1 \mid \cdot)$, which gives $0$, and trying to sum over variables. When every variable is fixed, no marginalisation is needed.

transcription.notes: Single-pass transcription from the official paper rendering; awaiting independent check. The network diagram is a raster image embedded in the official PDF (page 41) and is copied unchanged as Q64-1.png. The four conditional probability tables are transcribed as Markdown tables in the order printed: P(·) for U, then P(V|·), P(W|·) and P(Z|·). In the paper the P(V|·) and P(W|·) tables are drawn directly one above the other. The P(Z|·) table has separate row-label columns for V and W, reproduced here as two columns with empty headers. The PDF text layer places the table contents after the final sentence; the order used here follows the rendered page, where all tables come before the question sentence.

answerVerification.method: Author solve (not blind) compared with official key
answerVerification.notes: Python evaluates the factorised joint P(U)P(V|U)P(W|U)P(Z|V,W) from the transcribed CPTs: P(U=1, V=1, W=1, Z=1) = 0.5 × 0.5 × 1 × 0.5 = 0.125. As a consistency check on the transcribed tables, the 16 joint entries sum to 1. This matches the official key 0.125 to 0.125.
